name: Hyperscan
workload: Total wall-clock time to match Snort Talos (1,300 regexes) and Suricata ET-Open (2,800 regexes) rulesets against a 1GB real HTTP traffic trace (818,682 packets), single CPU core, comparing PCRE, PCRE2, RE2, and Hyperscan in single-regex (-s) and multi-regex parallel (-m) modes.
claimed_speedup: Table 5 (seconds, lower=better): Talos ruleset - PCRE 6942, PCRE2 394, RE2-s 1777, Hyperscan-s 173, RE2-m 29, Hyperscan-m 2.15. ET-Open - PCRE 12800, PCRE2 913, RE2-s 4696, Hyperscan-s 516, RE2-m 1116, Hyperscan-m 133. Paper states: 'Hyperscan-s outperforms PCRE, RE2-s, and PCRE2 by 40.1x, 10.3x, and 2.3x' (Talos); 'Hyperscan-m is 13.5x faster than RE2-m while it reveals 183.3x performance improvement over PCRE2' (Talos); 'Hyperscan-s shows 24.8x, 9.1x, and 1.8x speedups over PCRE, RE2-s, and PCRE2' (ET-Open); 'Hyperscan-m outperforms RE2-m and PCRE2 by 8.4x and 6.9x' (ET-Open). Separately, Hyperscan-ported Snort achieves 986 Mbps vs 113 Mbps for stock Snort (8.73x) on the same real traffic.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4; PCRE v8.41 and PCRE2 v10.32 built with JIT enabled; RE2 v2018-09-01; Hyperscan v5.0. Full optimization flags not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8180 CPU @ 2.50GHz, 48GB memory, single core used for evaluation
stars_or_usage: 5.5k stars; used in Snort/Suricata-class DPI, widely deployed in network security products
tradeoffs: x86-specific (SIMD/SSE/AVX) C API; requires precompiled pattern databases (compile step separate from scan); biggest wins are in multi-pattern/large-ruleset DPI workloads (6.9-183x over PCRE2) rather than single-pattern matching (2.3x over PCRE2); streaming mode has extra overhead vs block mode.
caveats: Benchmark was run and published by the paper's authors, several of whom (Intel, branchfree.org's Geoff Langdale) are Hyperscan's own developers, so despite NSDI peer review it is not fully independent. The real-world HTTP traffic trace ('obtained at a cloud service provider') is not public, so exact reproduction needs a substitute trace; no explicit public artifact/script repo for the Snort/ruleset harness was found, only library versions and hardware/compiler, so tier capped at B rather than A. Some ratios exceed 50x (e.g. 183.3x) but compiler/hardware/library versions are stated and it is not a debug/-O0 build, so the hard-rule auto-cap-to-C does not apply.

name: RE2
workload: Same NSDI'19 Hyperscan-paper experiment: total wall-clock time for single-regex serial matching (RE2-s) of Snort Talos (1,300 regexes) and Suricata ET-Open (2,800 regexes) rulesets against a 1GB real HTTP traffic trace, single CPU core.
claimed_speedup: RE2-s beats classic (non-JIT) PCRE v8.41: Talos 6942s -> 1777s (~3.9x); ET-Open 12800s -> 4696s (~2.7x) (derived from page data, Table 5). Paper explicitly states Hyperscan-s beats RE2-s by 10.3x/9.1x, implying RE2-s itself is faster than plain PCRE but far slower than PCRE2 (JIT): RE2-s (1777s/4696s) was actually slower than PCRE2 (394s/913s) in the same table, and RE2-m (1116s) was slower than PCRE2 (913s) on the larger ET-Open ruleset.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4; RE2 v2018-09-01; PCRE v8.41 (non-JIT, matched one-at-a-time per RE2/PCRE's API); full optimization flags not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8180 CPU @ 2.50GHz, 48GB memory, single core
stars_or_usage: 9.8k stars; used in production at Google since 2006 and widely elsewhere
tradeoffs: Linear-time guarantee (no catastrophic backtracking) trades away backreferences and lookaround; RE2's own README explicitly disclaims being a universal speed leader ('It is not a goal to be faster than all other engines under all circumstances'); in this benchmark RE2 loses outright to PCRE2's JIT compiler despite beating classic PCRE.
caveats: RE2's own repo/README and its historic benchlog files (benchlog/benchlog.c2, .mini, .r70, .wreck) only benchmark against classic PCRE on decade-old hardware (e.g. AMD Opteron 8214, MacPro1,1 circa 2008-2010) with no PCRE2 or std::regex comparison at all -- PCRE2 postdates most of those logs. No first-party or independent source found this session showing RE2 beating std::regex or PCRE2 specifically; the only numeric, methodologically-documented comparison located is the third-party NSDI'19 Hyperscan paper (same source used for the Hyperscan record above), where RE2 beats classic PCRE but not PCRE2. Baseline recorded here is PCRE (not in this project's suggested baseline list of std::regex/PCRE2), so baseline_in_list=false per the hard rules.
found_via: seed-record pass: data/wave0-seed/prompts/seed-05-regex-conc.txt; NSDI'19 paper https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi19/presentation/wang-xiang; RE2 repo benchlog/ and README checked directly for a std::regex/PCRE2 comparison but found none

name: CTRE (compile-time regular expressions)
workload: Raw `time`-command wall-clock comparison of egrep, CTRE, PCRE, and std::regex matching four regex patterns (e.g. 'ABCD|DEFGH|EFGHI|A{4,}', '[0-9a-fA-F]{8,16}', '^([0-9]{4,16})?[aA]', '([aAbB]{4,}|[xXyY]{4,}|[1234]{4,})0'), captured once with clang (clang-bench.txt) and once with gcc (gcc-bench.txt). No description of input size, test harness, or what program was actually timed.
claimed_speedup: clang-bench.txt: CTRE 10.093s vs std::regex 21m9.309s (~125x) on 'ABCD|DEFGH|EFGHI|A{4,}'; CTRE 14.197s vs std::regex 2m34.505s (~10.9x) on '[0-9a-fA-F]{8,16}'; CTRE 7.596s vs std::regex 7m54.793s (~62.5x) on '^([0-9]{4,16})?[aA]'; CTRE 59.864s vs std::regex 27m35.004s (~27.6x) on the alternation pattern. gcc-bench.txt shows smaller but still large gaps, e.g. CTRE 3.982s vs std::regex 0m55.058s (~13.8x) on the first pattern.
compiler_and_flags: clang (version unstated) for clang-bench.txt, gcc (version unstated) for gcc-bench.txt; no optimization flags stated.
stars_or_usage: 3.9k stars; used as a reference implementation for a C++ standards proposal (P1433) for compile-time regex
tradeoffs: Regex pattern must be a compile-time-known string (template/NTTP); needs recent compilers (clang 14+, gcc 9+, MSVC 16.11+); does not support callouts, comments, conditional patterns, control-char escapes, named characters, octal numbers, subroutines, or Unicode grapheme-cluster \X (per README's PCRE-syntax exception list).
caveats: Current README (v3) contains zero benchmark numbers, and the compile-time.re site's dedicated 'Performance graph' page (/graph/) is JS-rendered client-side and its underlying data could not be extracted via WebFetch this session. The only numeric evidence found is two stale, undocumented repo files (clang-bench.txt / gcc-bench.txt) with no compiler version, flags, hardware, or input description, and several ratios exceed 50x -- per the hard rules this unstated-methodology + implausible-ratio combination caps the tier at C. It is unclear which CTRE version/commit produced these files or whether they reflect the current v3 codebase.
found_via: seed-record pass: data/wave0-seed/prompts/seed-05-regex-conc.txt; repo files clang-bench.txt and gcc-bench.txt in github.com/hanickadot/compile-time-regular-expressions; compile-time.re homepage and /graph/ page checked for benchmarks

name: moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue
workload: Producer/consumer microbenchmarks on AWS 8-core (c1.xlarge, Xeon E5506 @2.13GHz) and 32-core (cc2.8xlarge, Xeon E5-2670 @2.60GHz) instances, varying thread counts, comparing moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue (with/without tokens, incl. bulk ops), boost::lockfree::queue, tbb::concurrent_queue, and a std::mutex-locked queue (LockBasedQueue), under balanced mixed producer/consumer and producer-only workloads.
claimed_speedup: Balanced 8-thread workload: moodycamel (with tokens) 795.01k ops/s vs boost::lockfree 647.96k ops/s (~1.2x) vs tbb::concurrent_queue 692.97k ops/s (~1.15x). Producer-only 8-thread throughput: moodycamel 65.56M ops/s vs boost::lockfree 289.71k ops/s (~226x, via bulk enqueue) vs tbb 936.20k ops/s (~70x). Weighted overall average ops/s/thread across all thread counts: moodycamel (incl. bulk) 19.04M vs boost::lockfree 4.07M (~4.7x) vs tbb 5.09M (~3.7x). LockBasedQueue (std::mutex+std::queue) shown separately degrading from 2.6us/op at 2 threads to 112us/op at 16 threads under contention.
compiler_and_flags: g++ on Ubuntu; exact g++ version and optimization flags (-O2/-O3 etc.) not stated on the blog page.
hardware: AWS c1.xlarge: 8-core Intel Xeon E5506 @ 2.13GHz; AWS cc2.8xlarge: 32-core Intel Xeon E5-2670 @ 2.60GHz; Ubuntu
stars_or_usage: 12.5k stars; packaged in vcpkg, used across many C++ game/systems projects
tradeoffs: Not linearizable across independent producers; not NUMA-aware; single-header C++11; the largest speedups (~70-226x) come from its bulk enqueue/dequeue API rather than single-item ops, where the advantage over boost::lockfree is closer to ~1.2x in this benchmark.
caveats: This is a first-party benchmark (author's own blog post plus the repo's own benchmarks/ directory), not an independent suite -- the schema's rule states project's-own-benchmark-with-partial-methodology is tier C, not B. Compiler version and optimization flags are not stated even though CPU models and OS are; the ~226x producer-only figure is a bulk-vs-non-bulk comparison, not like-for-like single-enqueue throughput. Data is from a 2014 blog post and has not been re-verified against current boost/TBB releases this session.
